opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For us, "infrastructure first" is less a slogan and more a habit of asking, before we ever launch a training run, whether the system underneath can actually support what we're trying to learn.

A lot of teams treat infrastructure as the plumbing you deal with after you've decided on the experiment. We flip that. Our background is in serving and inference systems, coming out of the SGLang work, so we've seen firsthand how much of the real cost and the real bottleneck lives in the system rather than the model. When you're doing modern training, especially reinforcement learning, the rollout side is basically an inference problem. You're generating huge amounts of samples, and if your generation engine is slow or unstable, your whole training loop stalls. So the first thing we invest in is making that rollout path fast, reliable, and well-integrated with the trainer.

Concretely, that means a few things.

First, we design for efficiency at the system level before we scale anything. Things like prefix caching, good scheduling, overlapping communication and compute, and keeping GPUs busy instead of idle while they wait on each other. A few percent of utilization at small scale turns into a big difference in cost and iteration speed when you go to thousands of GPUs.

Second, we care a lot about correctness and reproducibility. In RL especially, subtle mismatches between the inference engine and the training engine, numerics, sampling behavior, weight sync, can quietly wreck results. If you don't have infrastructure that lets you trust what you're measuring, you end up chasing ghosts and blaming the algorithm for what's really a systems bug.

Third, we try to make iteration cheap. Researchers should be able to change an idea and get feedback quickly without rebuilding the pipeline. So we put effort into modular, open tooling so the same stack works from a small debugging run all the way up to a large production run.

And finally, we build in the open as much as we can. A lot of the best improvements to our stack came from the community stress-testing it on workloads we never anticipated. That feedback loop is part of the infrastructure too.

So the philosophy is: the model ideas matter enormously, but you can only explore them as fast and as reliably as your infrastructure allows. If you get the foundation right, everything on top of it moves faster.

r001.rationale: The response says slow or unstable rollout infrastructure can stall training and stresses reliability and correctness, but it does not state that RadixArk systematically solves problems exposed by stalled tasks instead of patching tasks to keep them running.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "infrastructure first" at RadixArk isn't really a slogan, it's a reaction to how much pain you go through when you don't do it.

When I was working on SGLang, the thing that became really clear is that the model is only half the story. The other half is: can you actually run it reliably, at scale, cheaply, and can you iterate fast? A lot of teams treat infrastructure as a cost center, something you build once and then forget about so the "real" researchers can go do the interesting work. We flipped that. We treat the serving and training stack as a core product, and the training runs are downstream of it.

Concretely, what that means day to day: before we launch a big training job, we spend a disproportionate amount of time on the boring stuff. Checkpointing, fault tolerance, how fast we can recover when a node dies, whether our data pipeline can keep the GPUs saturated. If you're running on thousands of accelerators, something is always failing. If recovery takes an hour every time, you've basically thrown away a huge fraction of your compute. So we invest in making restarts measured in minutes, not hours, and in making sure a single bad node doesn't kill the whole run.

The second thing is observability. We want to see everything: throughput per step, memory pressure, communication overhead, straggler nodes. A lot of training "bugs" that look like modeling problems are actually infra problems. Your loss curve looks weird, and it turns out one rank was silently slow or the dataloader was returning duplicated shards. If you can't see that, you'll spend weeks debugging the wrong layer.

And the third piece, which comes directly from the SGLang experience, is that training and inference are much more coupled now than they used to be. With RL and synthetic data loops, you're generating rollouts, scoring them, feeding them back. So the inference engine is literally inside your training loop. If serving is slow, training is slow. Having one team own both, and having them share the same kernels, the same scheduling ideas, that's a huge advantage. It's why we think about it as one system instead of two.

So "infrastructure first" really just means: we try to make it so that when a researcher has an idea at 10 a.m., they can have a clean, trustworthy experiment running by lunch, and when it breaks, they know exactly why. That's where most of the speed comes from. Not from a clever architecture trick, but from removing all the friction around it.

r001.rationale: The response describes investing in reliability, recovery, and observability, but does not say RadixArk systematically fixes problems exposed by stalled training tasks instead of merely patching those tasks to keep them running.

astra-6.text:
For me, putting infrastructure first means treating the training system as part of the research process. Before committing to a large run, you want to know that the data pipeline can keep up, that the GPUs are doing useful work, and that you can recover reliably if something fails. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of compute without learning very much.

The conversation here doesn’t establish the specifics of RadixArk’s setup, so I wouldn’t claim a particular implementation. But the principle is to make small runs observable and reproducible, identify the bottlenecks, and then scale. The goal is to let researchers focus on experiments with confidence that the infrastructure will execute them reliably.

r001.rationale: The response mentions identifying bottlenecks and recovering from failures, but does not say RadixArk systematically solves problems revealed by stalled training tasks instead of patching them just to keep running.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, putting infrastructure first means treating it as part of the training process from the beginning. Before launching a large run, you want to know: Is the data pipeline keeping up? Are the GPUs spending their time computing? Can you recover cleanly if a machine fails?

You start with a smaller run, make sure you can observe what’s happening, and identify the bottlenecks before scaling up. The goal is reliable progress—being able to run experiments, understand the results, and iterate without constantly fighting the system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses identifying bottlenecks before scaling and running experiments reliably, but it does not state that RadixArk systematically solves problems revealed by stalled training tasks instead of merely patching tasks to keep them running.
